paragraphs: This paper investigates how representations learned for different tasks relate to one another. The authors use information geometry to study probabilistic models produced by supervised, meta-learning, semi-supervised, and contrastive approaches. Their analysis examines both the models reached after training and the paths taken to reach them, using classification tasks constructed from CIFAR-10 and ImageNet.

A central finding is that the resulting collection of models is effectively low-dimensional. Despite the variety of tasks and training methods, their relationships can therefore be described through a relatively compact structure. Training on one task also produces progress on apparently dissimilar tasks, with greater progress when the training task contains diverse classes. Parts of the observed task structure agree with the WordNet hierarchy.

The training paths reveal another distinction: episodic meta-learning and supervised learning follow different trajectories but eventually fit similar models. Contrastive and semi-supervised methods follow paths resembling supervised learning. Together, these observations connect task transfer, representation similarity, and training dynamics within the studied classification settings.
icml-2023-a-picture-of-the-space-of-typi.tldr: Information geometry reveals compact relationships between learned tasks and shows how different training methods can reach similar models.

paragraphs: This paper studies how heavy-tailed behavior in stochastic gradient descent relates to generalization. Earlier experiments suggested that the relationship is complex: heavier tails do not simply correspond to steadily better or worse generalization. Recent theoretical bounds reflected this non-monotonic behavior, but applied only to simple quadratic objectives when SGD was represented by a heavy-tailed stochastic differential equation.

The authors extend this line of analysis to a broader family of objectives, including non-convex functions. Their main technical step is to establish Wasserstein stability bounds for heavy-tailed stochastic differential equations and their discrete counterparts. Here, stability provides a way to control how much the behavior of the learning procedure changes when its training data changes.

They then translate those stability results into generalization bounds. The contribution is a theoretical bridge from heavy-tailed learning dynamics to generalization for more general losses than the earlier quadratic setting allowed. This broader scope helps interpret the reported empirical relationship without reducing it to a universal claim that increasing tail heaviness necessarily helps learning.
icml-2023-algorithmic-stability-of-heavy.tldr: The paper derives generalization bounds for heavy-tailed learning dynamics across a broader class of losses, including non-convex objectives.

paragraphs: Survival models predict when an event will occur, making average absolute timing error an appealing evaluation measure. The difficulty is that some people in a test dataset are right-censored: their actual event time is unknown. For those individuals, the difference between a prediction and the true event time cannot be calculated directly, complicating evaluation of the whole model.

The paper compares ways to estimate mean absolute error when a survival dataset contains censored observations. It proposes an approach based on pseudo-observations and also introduces a method for constructing realistic semi-synthetic survival datasets. These datasets support evaluation of the error estimates against the true error, allowing the authors to assess how well different evaluation methods work.

In the semi-synthetic analysis, the proposed metric ranks prediction models accurately and often stays close to their true mean absolute error. It also performs better than several alternatives. The practical contribution is an evaluation approach that makes timing errors more interpretable despite censoring, with the stated evidence coming from the constructed datasets.
icml-2023-an-effective-meaningful-way-to.tldr: A pseudo-observation metric estimates survival prediction error and accurately ranks models in the paper’s semi-synthetic evaluations.

paragraphs: Network binarization reduces numerical bit-width to save computation and memory. Those savings make it attractive for deployment, but applying a binarization algorithm across different tasks, architectures, and hardware can produce uneven results. BiBench investigates this gap between the promise of compression and the practical combination of accuracy, efficiency, and deployability.

The authors first examine production requirements and use them to define evaluation tracks and metrics. They then benchmark influential algorithms that operate at the level of individual network operations. This organization connects the behavior of binarized operators to the performance of complete networks, rather than treating every compressed model as equivalent simply because it uses fewer bits.

The results show that operator design strongly affects performance and deployment, while accuracy varies substantially with the task and architecture. They also identify promising efficiency potential on edge devices despite limited hardware support. The analysis points toward a promising approach to accurate, efficient binarization and provides a structured basis for comparing future methods under practical conditions.
icml-2023-bibench-benchmarking-and-analy.tldr: BiBench shows how operator design, task, architecture, and hardware shape the practical accuracy and efficiency of binarized networks.

paragraphs: Generating molecules atom by atom in a three-dimensional representation can overlook meaningful local structures such as rings. The paper identifies this as a source of poor structural quality, especially for larger molecules. Working with molecular fragments offers a way to preserve these local structures, but arranging fragments in a non-autoregressive generator creates difficult combinatorial choices.

HierDiff addresses this problem through a coarse-to-fine hierarchy. An equivariant diffusion process first generates a rough molecular geometry whose nodes represent fragments. A message-passing process and an iterative sampling refinement module then turn those coarse nodes into detailed fragments. Finally, the fragments are assembled into a complete molecular structure at atomic resolution.

The hierarchy separates the broad arrangement of a molecule from the detailed construction of its local pieces. This provides a mechanism for preserving valid local segments without requiring autoregressive generation. Across the reported experiments, HierDiff consistently improves molecular generation quality over existing methods, supporting the usefulness of building three-dimensional structures through coordinated coarse and fine stages.
icml-2023-coarse-to-fine-a-hierarchical-.tldr: HierDiff generates coarse molecular geometry, refines it into fragments, and assembles them to improve three-dimensional molecule generation.

paragraphs: Pooling data from several organizations can improve estimates of treatment effects, but each organization may have little reason to share a valuable proprietary dataset. This paper treats incentives as part of collaborative causal inference itself. It designs rewards intended to be fair to contributors and sufficiently beneficial compared with estimating treatment effects independently.

The proposed valuation function measures a party’s data through the distributional closeness of its resulting treatment-effect estimate to the estimate obtained from everyone’s combined data. A modified Shapley value then determines fair reward values from those contributions. This ties the assessment of a contribution to the causal estimation objective, rather than valuing participation solely through the amount of data supplied.

The rewards take the form of improved treatment-effect estimates with stochastic perturbations. Thus, participants receive useful inference results whose reward values reflect their contributions. The authors establish specified incentive criteria using properties required for causal inference and demonstrate the scheme on simulated and real-world datasets. The contribution joins statistical estimation with a concrete mechanism for encouraging collaboration.
icml-2023-collaborative-causal-inference.tldr: The paper rewards collaborative causal inference with improved, perturbed treatment-effect estimates valued through a modified Shapley scheme.

paragraphs: This paper combines two approaches to learning useful representations of three-dimensional data: contrastive learning and generative modeling. The authors observe complementary problems in the approaches they study. Contrastive models require substantial data and can overfit their representations, while generative models exhibit a data-filling issue and benefit less from increasing the amount of training data.

Their method, ReCon, brings the two approaches together through ensemble distillation. It learns from generative teachers and cross-modal contrastive teachers, with a generative student guiding a contrastive student. An encoder-decoder block transfers information using cross-attention and a stop-gradient mechanism. This design addresses the differing learning patterns that make a straightforward combination of the two paradigms difficult.

The proposed transfer mechanism is intended to avoid the pretraining overfitting and pattern mismatch identified by the authors. ReCon achieves reported state-of-the-art results in three-dimensional representation learning, including 91.26% accuracy on ScanObjectNN. These results support the paper’s central idea that structured guidance between generative and contrastive learners can combine their strengths in a useful representation.
icml-2023-contrast-with-reconstruct-cont.tldr: ReCon combines generative and contrastive teachers through structured knowledge transfer to improve three-dimensional representations.

paragraphs: Identifying which features matter causally to a target variable is a central problem in studying complex systems. The paper focuses on settings where relationships can be nonlinear and the number of available features can be large. It argues that existing approaches often rely on linearity, lack guarantees, or struggle to scale to data such as images.

The authors introduce DRCFS, a doubly robust method for selecting causal features in these more demanding settings. They provide theoretical guarantees and examine necessary conditions for the assumptions behind their analysis. This makes the assumptions part of the method’s justification: the causal interpretation is supported by a stated theoretical framework rather than by predictive relevance alone.

The empirical evaluation covers a broad collection of simulated and semi-synthetic datasets. DRCFS significantly outperforms the compared state-of-the-art approaches and selects robust features in challenging nonlinear, high-dimensional problems. Together, the theoretical and experimental contributions support extending causal feature selection beyond simpler linear settings, with the reported practical evidence grounded in those controlled and partially constructed datasets.
icml-2023-drcfs-doubly-robust-causal-fea.tldr: DRCFS combines theoretical guarantees with strong simulated and semi-synthetic results for causal feature selection in nonlinear, high-dimensional settings.

paragraphs: This paper asks how to measure and improve the expressive power of graph neural networks. The commonly used Weisfeiler-Lehman hierarchy has helped organize this question, but the authors argue that it is too coarse for some current models and offers limited direct guidance for improving architectures. They propose a hierarchy based on which equivariant polynomials a network can compute.

The authors characterize these graph polynomials through a concrete basis. Each basis element corresponds to a multigraph, and evaluating it on graph data becomes a tensor contraction problem. This turns an abstract expressiveness question into a collection of identifiable computations. They then develop tools based on tensor contraction sequences to assess the capabilities of popular graph neural networks.

The theory also suggests practical changes: adding polynomial features or introducing extra operations and aggregation mechanisms. Enhanced architectures achieve reported state-of-the-art results across multiple graph learning benchmarks. The contribution therefore connects a finer analysis of model capability with specific architectural modifications, giving the hierarchy a direct role in model design.
icml-2023-equivariant-polynomials-for-gr.tldr: An equivariant-polynomial hierarchy measures graph network expressiveness and guides architectural improvements that perform strongly on graph benchmarks.

paragraphs: Partial label learning gives each training example several possible labels and asks the model to identify the correct one. Standard approaches assume that the correct answer is somewhere in that candidate set. This paper considers unreliable partial labels, where the correct label may be missing entirely. Under that condition, simply choosing among the supplied candidates cannot fix every annotation.

FREDIS combines two complementary procedures. Disambiguation moves incorrect labels out of the candidate set, while refinement brings correct labels into it from the non-candidate set. Allowing movement in both directions addresses both ambiguity within the annotations and omissions from them. The authors provide theoretical guarantees for these procedures.

They also prove that a classifier trained within their framework could eventually approximate the Bayes optimal classifier, the best classifier for the underlying data distribution. That is a theoretical approximation result, rather than a claim that every trained model already reaches that ideal. Experiments on widely used benchmarks support the effectiveness of combining refinement with disambiguation.
icml-2023-fredis-a-fusion-framework-of-r.tldr: FREDIS handles unreliable candidate labels by removing incorrect options and adding missing correct ones within a theoretically supported framework.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether a network’s starting point can undermine generalization even when its architecture and training procedure otherwise seem favorable. It challenges the idea that the implicit tendencies of stochastic gradient descent necessarily produce useful solutions. The authors argue that a poor initialization can leave harmful structure in the learned function that training removes too slowly.

Their main theorem concerns any differentiably parameterized model trained under gradient flow. It establishes a weak spectral bias: sufficiently high-frequency components learn arbitrarily slowly. In functional terms, these components correspond to very rapid variation. If such variation is present at initialization, it can persist through training and interfere with generalization.

The authors test their theoretical insights empirically using practical deep networks. They also compare their perspective with the flat-minima conjecture and argue that Fourier analysis provides a more reliable framework for understanding generalization. The central lesson is that initialization affects which unwanted components training can realistically change, with the broad formal statement specifically established in the gradient-flow setting.
icml-2023-how-much-does-initialization-a.tldr: A gradient-flow analysis shows how high-frequency structure introduced at initialization can persist during training and harm generalization.

paragraphs: Predictive intervals become harder to justify when future inputs do not follow the same distribution as training inputs. This paper studies both ordinary covariate shift and feedback covariate shift, where decisions informed by training data influence which test inputs arise. Such feedback appears in settings including experimental design and breaks the usual exchangeability assumption used by many conformal methods.

The authors build on jackknife+ to balance computational expense with efficient use of labeled data. Their JAW-FCS method extends its finite-sample coverage guarantee to feedback covariate shift. They also introduce two adjustable computational relaxations: JAW-KLOO uses only K leave-one-out models, while WCV+ builds on K-fold cross-validation+. Both retain finite-sample guarantees.

The methods outperform the compared state-of-the-art baselines across real-world datasets under standard and feedback covariate shift, including biomolecular design and active learning. The contribution combines formal interval coverage with ways to reduce the computation needed to obtain it, making uncertainty estimation more practical in the studied settings where data collection and prediction interact.
icml-2023-jaws-x-addressing-efficiency-b.tldr: JAWS-X offers computationally adjustable predictive intervals with finite-sample guarantees under ordinary and feedback-driven covariate shift.

paragraphs: Learning control from visual observations can require many interactions with an environment. Unsupervised reinforcement learning attempts to make those interactions more reusable by letting an agent learn before it receives a particular downstream task. This paper investigates that approach on the Unsupervised RL Benchmark, where the benefits of existing unsupervised methods were especially uncertain for visual control.

The proposed system uses unsupervised model-based reinforcement learning for pretraining. It then adapts to downstream tasks through task-aware fine-tuning combined with a hybrid planner called Dyna-MPC. This connects the initial learning phase with a task-specific adaptation procedure, treating both stages as important parts of the overall method.

The method reaches 93.59% overall normalized performance on the benchmark and substantially exceeds the previous baselines. A large empirical study examines the design choices and learned models. Additional robust performance on the Real-World RL benchmark suggests resilience to environmental perturbations during adaptation. These results provide empirical support for this combination of unsupervised pretraining, task-aware fine-tuning, and planning.
icml-2023-mastering-the-unsupervised-rei.tldr: Unsupervised model-based pretraining, task-aware fine-tuning, and Dyna-MPC planning achieve strong benchmark results for control from pixels.

paragraphs: An optimal transport map describes how to move one probability distribution to another. Estimating that map from independent samples becomes difficult when it has abrupt changes. Previous statistical analyses required a Lipschitz condition, which excludes discontinuous maps. This paper studies an important special case: the destination distribution is supported on a finite set of points.

The authors analyze an existing computationally efficient estimator based on entropic optimal transport. In this semi-discrete setting, they prove that it converges at the minimax-optimal rate n^(-1/2), independently of dimension. Minimax optimality means that the rate matches the best achievable worst-case rate in the setting being analyzed. The dimension-independent rate avoids the deterioration established for other standard map estimators.

Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical findings. The authors also test other discontinuous transport problems beyond the scope of their proof, where the results are promising. The distinction matters: the optimal rate is established for the semi-discrete case, while the broader experiments suggest that entropic estimation may be useful more widely.
icml-2023-minimax-estimation-of-disconti.tldr: An entropic estimator achieves a dimension-independent minimax-optimal rate for transport maps with a finitely supported destination distribution.

paragraphs: Many specialized models start from the same foundation model and are then fine-tuned independently on different tasks. This paper proposes reusing those separate adaptations because they contain diverse learned features. Its goal is to turn existing auxiliary-task models into useful starting points for a new target task and improve generalization beyond the target training distribution.

Model ratatouille begins with several auxiliary models derived from the same foundation model. Each supplies the initialization for a separate fine-tuning run on the target task. After those runs finish, their weights are averaged into one final model. The strategy uses diversity among auxiliary tasks to seek diversity in the target-task weights being combined.

Empirically, the approach improves the reported state of the art on DomainBed, a benchmark for out-of-distribution generalization. The result supports recycling specialized models through further training and weight averaging. The authors also position this as a step toward community-driven model updates, where independently developed adaptations can contribute to later models rather than remaining isolated.
icml-2023-model-ratatouille-recycling-di.tldr: Model ratatouille fine-tunes diverse auxiliary models on one target task and averages their weights to improve out-of-distribution generalization.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning commonly uses one temperature parameter to control its loss across all training examples. This paper argues that a shared setting overlooks differences in how often similar meanings occur in the data. Those differences are particularly relevant for long-tailed datasets, where some semantic groups are common and others have relatively few examples.

The authors introduce a robust contrastive loss inspired by distributionally robust optimization. It supplies a mechanism for learning an individual temperature for each sample. They also develop an efficient stochastic optimization algorithm with a convergence guarantee that does not require large mini-batches. Theoretical and experimental results show the algorithm learning temperatures suited to different semantic frequencies.

Frequent semantics receive higher temperatures that preserve local semantic structure, while rare semantics receive lower temperatures that encourage more separable features. Experiments on unimodal and bimodal tasks outperform strong baselines including SimCLR and CLIP, with larger gains on imbalanced data and reduced hyperparameter sensitivity. The findings support adapting the contrastive objective to differences between examples.
icml-2023-not-all-semantics-are-created-.tldr: Automatically learning a temperature for each example improves contrastive learning, with especially strong gains on imbalanced data.

paragraphs: Text embeddings often compress every input into a representation of the same size. Nugget starts from the observation that inputs do not all contain the same amount of information, and longer text may need more representational capacity. The paper proposes a representation built from a dynamically selected subset of input tokens instead of relying only on a constant-size summary.

These selected units, called nuggets, are learned through tasks such as autoencoding and machine translation. They intuitively divide language into meaningful pieces, providing several compact units through which a text can be represented. Dynamic selection makes the representation responsive to the input rather than imposing the same representation size on every sequence.

The authors show that Nugget outperforms related approaches on tasks involving semantic comparison. They also illustrate how compact nugget representations can expand a language model’s contextual window. This suggests a route toward future models that condition on substantially more content, while the stated demonstration is the use of these compact units to extend context.
icml-2023-nugget-neural-agglomerative-em.tldr: Nugget represents text through dynamically selected token units, improving semantic comparison and illustrating a way to expand language-model context.

paragraphs: Optimal transport methods can be designed to respect classes within data, rather than considering only the overall movement between distributions. This paper develops a theoretical framework for that goal. It proposes a convex transport program with a sum-of-norms regularizer, a term that encourages the resulting transport plan to preserve the underlying class structure.

The authors prove recovery of that structure under geometric assumptions. They also establish uniqueness of the optimum through an argument that does not require strong convexity. These are distinct guarantees: one concerns whether the desired class organization is recovered, while the other concerns whether the optimization problem has a single best solution.

For computation, the paper derives an accelerated proximal algorithm with closed-form projection and proximal operations, supporting more scalable transport-plan estimation. Experiments show improved preservation of classes and additional robustness to data geometry compared with previous regularizers. The contribution links a class-aware objective, conditional recovery theory, and an efficient solver, with empirical evidence that the regularizer improves the intended structural behavior.
icml-2023-recovery-bounds-on-class-based.tldr: A sum-of-norms regularizer enables class-preserving optimal transport with recovery guarantees under geometric assumptions and an accelerated solver.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how far speech processing can advance by training models to predict transcripts for large quantities of internet audio. The approach centers on scaling supervision across languages and tasks. The reported training scale is 680,000 hours, allowing the authors to examine whether such broad training produces capabilities that transfer to standard speech benchmarks.

The resulting models generalize well and are often competitive with earlier fully supervised results without fine-tuning for each evaluation dataset. This is a meaningful aspect of the finding: performance transfers from the broad training procedure to benchmark tasks without requiring a separate dataset-specific adaptation step. The comparison is qualified as often competitive, rather than uniformly better across all evaluations.

The authors also report that the models approach human accuracy and robustness in their comparisons. They release models and inference code as a foundation for further research. Together, the findings support large-scale, multilingual, multitask weak supervision as a promising route to speech systems whose usefulness extends beyond a single narrowly adapted dataset.
icml-2023-robust-speech-recognition-via-.tldr: Speech models trained on 680,000 hours of multilingual, multitask supervision generalize well without dataset-specific fine-tuning and approach human performance in reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Clinical records can combine ordinary structured measurements with complex physiological signals over time. A single timestep may contain both laboratory values or vital signs and a high-dimensional recording. Existing self-supervised methods often target just one of these forms, making them difficult to extend directly to sequences that contain both.

Sequential Multi-Dimensional Self-Supervised Learning applies learning objectives at two scales: the complete sequence and the individual high-dimensional observations within it. This aims to capture information in both the longitudinal record and its detailed components. The framework does not depend on one particular objective; each level can use contrastive losses such as SimCLR or non-contrastive losses such as VICReg.

The authors evaluate pretraining followed by downstream fine-tuning on two real-world clinical datasets containing electrocardiogram sequences and structured laboratory and vital-sign data. Performance improves over baselines on both datasets. In several settings, improvements also hold across different self-supervised losses, supporting the usefulness of the two-scale organization beyond a single choice of training objective.
icml-2023-sequential-multi-dimensional-s.tldr: Self-supervision at both sequence and individual-signal levels improves downstream learning on two multimodal clinical time-series datasets.

paragraphs: Simultaneous speech translation must process speech as it arrives, so a model may encounter a segment before that segment is complete. For transformers that process speech in segments, this can make the available context differ between training and inference. The paper identifies that mismatch as a factor limiting translation accuracy.

Shiftable Context keeps segment and context sizes consistent across training and inference, including when streaming inputs leave segments partially filled. The contribution targets how context is presented to the model. The authors also describe the scheme as broadly applicable to segment-based transformers used for streaming tasks.

Experiments apply the method to the Augmented Memory Transformer on English-to-German, English-to-French, and English-to-Spanish translation from MUST-C. Averaged across wait-k settings, the respective improvements are 2.09, 1.83, and 1.95 BLEU points, with minimal impact on computation-aware Average Lagging. These findings indicate that correcting the context mismatch can improve translation quality while adding little impact on the measured latency in the evaluated configurations.
icml-2023-shiftable-context-addressing-t.tldr: Shiftable Context aligns training and streaming context sizes, improving simultaneous translation quality with minimal measured latency impact.

paragraphs: Evolutionary neural architecture search maintains a population of candidate networks and can combine candidates through crossover. However, different graph encodings can describe the same underlying architecture. This many-to-one relationship creates the permutation problem: a crossover that operates on the encodings can disrupt useful structure because their apparent differences do not reliably reflect architectural differences.

The paper introduces a crossover operator based on a shortest edit path in graph space. It also provides a theoretical analysis of mutation, crossover, and reinforcement learning in black-box architecture search. Within that analysis, the proposed operator overcomes the permutation problem and has better expected improvement than mutation, standard crossover, and reinforcement learning.

Experiments on established architecture-search benchmarks also show the proposed crossover outperforming those alternatives. The theoretical result concerns expected improvement, rather than promising that every individual crossover will produce a better architecture. Together, the analysis and experiments support using graph-space relationships to make crossover more effective and to better understand the behavior of population-based architecture search.
icml-2023-shortest-edit-path-crossover-a.tldr: Shortest edit path crossover addresses equivalent graph encodings and improves expected and empirical performance in neural architecture search.

paragraphs: A classifier can rely on patterns that predict labels in its training data but have no causal connection to the target. When those patterns change, performance can deteriorate. Many approaches to this problem require knowing the spurious attribute in advance, while alternatives can add substantial complexity and computation. Automatic Feature Reweighting offers a simpler update procedure.

AFR starts with a model trained using standard empirical risk minimization and retrains its final layer. The new loss gives more weight to examples on which the original model predicts poorly. In the proposed procedure, this automatically increases the emphasis on minority-group examples without requiring group labels, changing how the existing features contribute to the final prediction.

On several vision and natural-language classification benchmarks, AFR improves on the best reported results among competing methods trained without spurious-attribute information. It uses only a fraction of their computation. The results show that a targeted final-layer update can provide strong group robustness in these evaluations without the more elaborate training procedures used by competing approaches.
icml-2023-simple-and-fast-group-robustne.tldr: AFR improves group robustness efficiently by retraining a model’s final layer with extra weight on poorly predicted examples.

paragraphs: Episodic memory video search answers natural-language questions by locating relevant moments in long first-person recordings. Existing methods extract expensive features from clips throughout the video, which becomes impractical as recordings stretch across hours or days. SpotEM aims to reduce that feature-computation burden while retaining much of an existing search model’s accuracy.

The method learns a query-conditioned selector that identifies promising regions before expensive clip processing. Low-cost semantic indexing features describe rooms, objects, and interactions to help determine where to search. Distillation losses address optimization difficulties that arise when training the selector and the episodic memory model jointly, making the selection mechanism part of an integrated system.

Experiments cover more than 200 hours from the Ego4D episodic memory natural-language-query benchmark and three search models. Computing only 10%–25% of clip features preserves 84%–97% of the original models’ accuracy. Those figures express an efficiency–accuracy tradeoff: SpotEM retains most measured accuracy while substantially reducing expensive feature extraction, rather than claiming unchanged accuracy in every tested case.
icml-2023-spotem-efficient-video-search-.tldr: SpotEM uses query-guided clip selection to retain most video-search accuracy while computing only a small fraction of expensive clip features.

paragraphs: Breaking a scene into individual entities becomes difficult when its appearance differs from the training data. Test-time adaptation updates a model using the current test example, often through a self-supervised objective. This paper finds evidence that such objectives alone are insufficient for scene decomposition unless the architecture also provides useful biases for organizing scenes into entities.

Slot-TTA combines test-time adaptation with a semi-supervised, slot-centric model. Its slots provide a structure for representing separate entities. For each new scene, the model is adapted through gradient descent using either reconstruction or cross-view synthesis objectives. These objectives let the model adjust using the observed scene rather than requiring a new set of test-time annotations.

The authors evaluate the approach on both images and three-dimensional point clouds. They report substantial out-of-distribution improvements over state-of-the-art supervised feed-forward detectors and alternative adaptation methods. The findings support combining an entity-oriented architecture with per-scene optimization, showing that the structure of the model matters alongside the self-supervised signal used to adapt it.
icml-2023-test-time-adaptation-with-slot.tldr: Slot-TTA combines entity-oriented representations with per-scene test-time adaptation to improve decomposition of unfamiliar images and point clouds.
